title: Maximum Number of Visible Points
statement:
You stand still at `location = [posx, posy]` on a grid, and `points[i] = [xi, yi]` are points with integer coordinates. You may turn to face any direction. Directions are measured in degrees counterclockwise from due east (the positive x direction); if you face direction `d`, you see every point whose direction from you lies in the closed range `[d - angle/2, d + angle/2]`.

- Several points may share a coordinate, and each counts separately.
- Points exactly at your location are always seen, whatever way you face.
- Points never block one another.

Return the largest number of points you can see at once.
signature: int visiblePoints(List<List<Integer>> points, int angle, List<Integer> location)
notes:
## Intuition

Only a point's direction matters, so turn each point into its polar angle around `location` (in degrees). A view of width `angle` then covers one arc of directions, and the best arc can always be slid until its clockwise edge rests on some point. After sorting the angles, the points inside an arc are a contiguous run, which a sliding window counts in one pass. Points at your own location have no direction; count them separately and add them at the end. The brute force tries each point as the clockwise edge and counts the rest, which is O(n²).

## Approach

1. Count points equal to `location` in `same`; for every other point push `atan2(dy, dx)` in degrees into `angles`.
2. Sort `angles`, then append each angle plus 360 so an arc that crosses the ±180° seam becomes a plain run.
3. Move `right` across `angles`; while `angles[right] - angles[left]` exceeds `angle` (with a 1e-9 tolerance), advance `left`.
4. The window `left..right` is one visible arc; keep its largest size in `best`.
5. Return `best + same`.

## Example 1, step by step

From `[1, 1]`, the points `[2, 1]`, `[2, 2]`, `[3, 3]` have angles `0`, `45`, `45`. Sorted and doubled: `[0, 45, 45, 360, 405, 405]`. With `right = 2` the spread is `45 - 0 <= 90`, so the window holds 3 points. At `right = 3` the spread `360 - 0` is too wide and `left` moves to 1; `360 - 45` is still too wide, and so on, so no later window beats 3. `same = 0`, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for sorting; the window moves each pointer at most 2n times.
- Space: O(n) for the doubled `angles` list.

## Pitfalls

- Points at your location have no defined angle; including them would misplace them and lose them when the view turns.
- The range is inclusive, and degrees from `atan2` carry rounding error, so compare against `angle + 1e-9`, not `angle` exactly.
- Without the +360 copies, a view that straddles the west direction (where `atan2` jumps from 180 to -180) is missed.
- Repeated points share an angle; keep every copy, since each one counts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `px`, `py` | your location |
| `same` | points exactly at your location |
| `angles` | sorted directions in degrees, then the same list shifted by 360 |
| `count` | number of points not at your location |
| `left`, `right` | ends of the current arc in `angles` |
| `best` | most directional points seen in one arc |
